name: Field watch

lead: A field watch is a simple, hard-wearing wristwatch descended from watches issued to soldiers: a clear dial with large numerals, a modest case and often a canvas or leather strap.
People wear one as a low-key accessory that makes an outfit look deliberate and put together without being flashy. Its straightforward design suits casual and smart-casual clothing alike.

paras: Wearers pair it with a nylon, canvas or leather strap on the wrist as an everyday watch. It is usually chosen as a single understated accessory rather than part of a layered jewellery look.
There is no physical risk in wearing one. Antique military watches from the early twentieth century may have radium-painted dials, which are radioactive.

angle.text: A field watch gives the wrist a clean, practical accent that works with casual and smart-casual outfits. People use it as a single, understated accessory.

lead: A field watch is a utilitarian wristwatch derived from the timepieces soldiers wore in the field. Wristwatches were first worn by military men in the late nineteenth century, and the First World War accelerated adoption as trench warfare demanded precise timing [1][2].

Early service watches in the trenches had luminous dials and unbreakable glass, and the British War Office began issuing wristwatches to combatants in 1917 [1][2]. After the war the wristwatch became a mass-market item for men [1].

In style terms, people wear field watches for a clear, no-nonsense dial and an unfussy, rugged character that suits casual clothing. Watches in general are treated as both timekeepers and accessories valued for design [1].
infobox: Military service watches, late 19th to early 20th century [1][2]
Legible dial, luminous markers, rugged case, strap

paras: British officers used wristwatches in colonial campaigns in the 1880s, and a campaign watch for soldiers was later produced by Mappin and Webb [1]. In the First World War, trench watches combined pocket-watch features such as hinged covers with wearing on the wrist, and makers such as Omega, Longines, Elgin and Rolex supplied them [2].
Typical trench watches had enamel dials with wide white numerals and radium-painted hour hands, and some had mesh shrapnel guards [2]. Radium dials are radioactive [2].
Field-watch styling follows the same priorities as service watches: legibility, durability and low visibility of ornament [2].
In style discussion, a field watch is one option among accessories, chosen for versatility with casual clothing and its understated look.
